\subsection{Which objects are value objects}
\seclabel{revival-object-kinds}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] The opening section of \chapref{objects}, its list of
the kinds of objects.
\item[Change] Its sentence on the value objects named booleans, numeric
literals, IEEE floating-point numbers and integers; it now names integers of
every precision and rational numbers too.
Its sentence on the reference objects named arbitrary-precision numbers and
aggregates such as arrays, lists and sets; it now names strings and the
aggregates.
The passage gains one box.
The rule of strict equivalence (\secref{equivalence}) is unchanged: values of
different types are never strictly equivalent, value objects of one type are
when their fields are, a binary word by its bit pattern, and reference objects
only when they are one object.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows two
decisions of the revival.
By the first, of 6~November 2026, the values of the arbitrary-precision integer
and rational types are value objects: \library\ declare the arbitrary-precision
integer as a value object, and the sentence's own list called integers value
objects and arbitrary-precision numbers reference objects, so the text
disagreed with itself and with the library; the library's declaration is the
deliberate word.
By the second, of 6 and 7~November 2026, strictly equivalent means the rule of
\secref{equivalence} on both implementations, with no special case for any type,
and strings are reference objects: \library\ declare every kind of string as an
object without the \KWD{value} modifier, so two strings are strictly equivalent
only when they are one object, and their text equality is their own \EXP{=}.
The Working Draft of February 2011 named no kind for strings, and the
team's implementations compared two flat strings by their text and two ropes
by identity.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md}, section~2.4, and
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/string-equivalence-2026-11-06.md} in the
revival's repository.
\item[Effect] Both implementations answer \EXP{\sequiv} by the rule, and both
read the \KWD{value} modifier.
\Library\ declare the rational type's object and the two numeral objects of the
interpreter as value objects.
The departures:
the interpreter gives a floating-point numeral bound to a variable of type
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} the type of the numeral object, so it is not strictly
equivalent to a computed \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} value of the same bits;
an integer numeral is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} value in the interpreter, by its magnitude, and a numeral
object to the compiled type checker, so a numeral
compared with a typed value can answer differently on the two paths;
the compiled path's own library, used until the one library replaces it,
answers \EXP{\sequiv} on values of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64},
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, on strings and on booleans by
\EXP{=} before it
reaches the rule, so there two equal strings built apart are strictly
equivalent and \EXP{0.0} is strictly equivalent to \EXP{-0.0} (row~908 of the
revival's gap ledger);
and \library\ declare \EXP{=} on pairs and triples only, so two tuples of four
or more elements are equal only when they are strictly equivalent, and two such
tuples of equal strings built apart are not equal (row~923 of the revival's
gap ledger).
The answers are gated by \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleWalk.fss},
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/ValueObjectCC64Walk.fss} and, for the compiled
helper, by \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleCompiled.fss}.

lines 39--43 and 52--54:
\begin{quote}
Most objects with simple standard types,
such as booleans,
numeric literals,
IEEE floating-point numbers,
and integers are value objects.
\end{quote}
\begin{quote}
Reference objects include
arbitrary-precision numbers
and aggregates such as arrays, lists and sets.
\end{quote}

A return to the original sentences would need \library\ to declare the
arbitrary-precision integer and the rational object without the \KWD{value}
modifier, so that two of their values built apart are never strictly
equivalent, and would leave the kind of strings unnamed.

== explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-29.md:332-401, the item at :347-360

**Rung N**

9. **N1 (consequential). The numeral types as plain value objects with Fortress fields, in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `.fss` beside `Ratio`.** `trait Numeral extends Number comprises { NaturalNumeral, RadixPointNumeral }` declares the four getters abstract; `value object NaturalNumeral(digits: ZZ32, radix: ZZ32, digitValue: ZZ) extends Numeral`, whose `fractionDigits` is 0; `value object RadixPointNumeral(digits: ZZ32, fractionDigits: ZZ32, radix: ZZ32, digitValue: ZZ) extends Numeral`. No binding: walk builds one by its constructor, found as walk's loader finds the library's exceptions (`interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java:281-286`, `getRootValue`). In `FortressBuiltin`, a native component, an object holds no field under walk (the mechanism of row 926, `BuildNativeEnvironment`; the row itself is closed, for `File`, which ceased to be native), so they leave it. The way not taken: section 2.
10. **N2. The checker's names switch by library**, as `CHARACTER` does (`compiler/Types.java:78-91`): `INT_LITERAL` and `FLOAT_LITERAL` name the prelude's `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` under the compiler's libraries and `FortressLibrary`'s `NaturalNumeral` and `RadixPointNumeral` under the one library. Default: so. The way not taken: rename the prelude's two traits, an edit of the prelude (P-37).
11. **N3. The getters' names and types:** `digits`, `fractionDigits`, `radix`, `digitValue`, the names the prototype proposed (section 7.1), `ZZ32` for the first three and `ZZ` for the value, which a 20-digit numeral needs; `Numeral` extends `Number`, as `IntLiteral` does today, so the library's `excludes` clauses and P-160's Meet Rule readings stand with the names changed. Default: so. The ways not taken: the Draft's letters `n`, `m`, `r`, `v`, which the specification keeps beside each name; `Numeral` outside `Number`.
12. **N4 (consequential; point 3). `RadixPointNumeral` declares `asFloat`, by one rounding, as `NaturalNumeral` does.** Section 2.
13. **N5. One rounding by a new pair of helpers,** a rational `v / r^m` correctly rounded to a double and to a float, in an existing helper class of the float arithmetic or a new one, bound by P-58's form, called by `RR64`'s and `RR32`'s coercions and by both numeral types' `asFloat`; walk's Java conversions call the same Java methods, so the two paths round alike. The prototype's `roundToDouble` and `roundToFloat` in the code generator are the precedent (its section 1, step 3). Default: so. The way not taken: `QQ`'s `asFloat`, `asFloat(num) / asFloat(den)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:656`), which rounds up to three times.
14. **N6. Walk's choice of a declaration reads a numeral argument as the checker does.** A declaration whose parameter at that position is the numeral's own type, or its default, fits the numeral as it is, and the default ranks as no coercion; the most specific of those that fit as they are wins (P-49); if none fits, the coercion attempt runs, and a tie that only numerals make reads each at its default (`Specification/basic/inference.tex`, "A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie", widened by P-173 to float numerals, which read `RR64`). So `x + 1` runs `ZZ32`'s `+` as today, `u = 0` for `u: NN32` runs `NN32`'s pair, `1.0 s` runs `RR64`'s juxtaposition, and `1/2 = 0.5` runs `QQ`'s pair. Default: so. The way not taken: walk's float numeral an `RR64` at evaluation, way F-c, which his default of item 446 declined.
15. **N7. Where walk converts, and how.** At a chosen declaration's parameter, a typed binding, a field and a declared return type, the checker's places, a numeral converts from its exact value: into the eight number types in walk's Java, by the same conversion as the library's coercion, a numeral out of the type's range refused at the place when it runs, as walk refuses one at a binding today (row 325's walk half); into a numeral type as the numeral object; into a program's type through its coercion from the numeral type, called with the numeral object, its result kept for the site so that a site gives one object (review-queue item 440's default); else refused. Elsewhere, an untyped binding, `Any`, `Object`, `Number` or an unbounded type parameter, it takes its default, as F-74 gives it for integers today. A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default holding them all, by a hook at the head of `EvaluatorBase.inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction` (`EvaluatorBase.java:72-94`), not at its three reads of a value's type, which are G's. Default: so. The ways not taken: a numeral object at every evaluation, which every `i + 1` would pay; conversion at bindings and fields only, as P-172's text names, which would leave a return of `QQ`, `RR32`, `NN32` or `NN64` unconverted.
16. **N8. The pairs, kept and completed.** Every coercion from a numeral type has its pair both ways: the eight number types each with `NaturalNumeral`, `RR32` gaining its coercion from it (P-76; probe 1), and `QQ`, `RR64` and `RR32` each with `RadixPointNumeral`: 11 coercions, 11 pairs at the number types and 11 at the numeral types, each pair's body converting and comparing as the library's do today (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:418`). Default: so. Under walk a pair's body runs with the numeral object; on the compiled path its fold waits for the switch-over (fork F6).
17. **N9. SEQV of two numeral objects inside a coercion's body compares their reduced values,** `digitValue / radix^fractionDigits`, so `2.5` and `2.50` are strictly equivalent there and `0.1_2` and `0.5` are too (P-168's one exception; review-queue item 445's default); walk's rule for value objects field by field takes the two types as its exception. Default: so.
18. **N10. A numeral object prints as the Draft writes a numeral,** its digits in its radix with the radix point after `digits - fractionDigits` of them and `_r` where the radix is not ten, so `C.8_16` in gives `C.8_16` out (the judgement's appendix); a numeral that took its default prints as its type does, `"" 2.50` giving `2.5`. Default: so.
19. **N11. Walk's glue classes of the two objects stay in the tree, unused,** `interpreter/glue/prim/IntLiteral.java` and `FloatLiteral.java`, as climb batch 28's rung R left its own (its fork R3); walk's value classes `FIntLiteral` and `FFloatLiteral` are N's to keep, rework or replace. Default: so; the removal is the names batch's clean-up.
20. **N12. The tests whose answer the design drops.** `tests/XXXRoundNearTieNumeral.fss` asserts 3 and 3 for `round(2.50000000000000001)` and `round(3.49999999999999999)`, where P-173's tie reading gives 2 and 4 on both paths (row 360, closed): it becomes a plain guard under a name of its topic that asserts 2 and 4, by `tests-writing.md`'s promotion steps. `tests/IntLiteralValue.fss` goes with row 578 and the object. `XXXNumeralFloatRungP` (row 443), `XXXNumeralWithNN32` (row 484) and `XXXRadixTenPointNumeral` (row 361) are promoted where your change makes them pass. `XXXextendIntLiteral` and `XXXextendFloatLiteral` name the new types, still refused. 1	(* The compiled helper of SEQV answers by the rule of objects.tex, section "Object Equivalence": values of different types are never equivalent, value objects and tuples compare field by field, floats by their bits, and reference objects, strings among them, only with themselves. *)
     2	component StrictEquivalenceRuleCompiled
     3	export Executable
     4	
     5	sEq(a: Any, b: Any): Boolean = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.equality.sEquiv")
     6	
     7	object Pt(x: ZZ32, y: ZZ32) end
     8	value object VPlain(a: ZZ32, b: ZZ32) end
     9	value object CC64(re: RR64, im: RR64) end
    10	object RC64(re: RR64, im: RR64) end
    11	
    12	numbers(): () = do
    13	  i: ZZ32 = 3
    14	  j: ZZ32 = 3
    15	  l: ZZ64 = 3
    16	  r: RR64 = 3.0
    17	  assert(sEq(i, j), "two ZZ32 3s")
    18	  assert(NOT sEq(i, l), "a ZZ32 3 and a ZZ64 3")
    19	  assert(NOT sEq(i, r), "a ZZ32 3 and an RR64 3.0")
    20	  zero: RR64 = 0.0
    21	  nz: RR64 = -0.0
    22	  nan: RR64 = zero / zero
    23	  assert(NOT sEq(zero, nz), "0.0 and -0.0")
    24	  assert(sEq(nan, nan), "a NaN with itself")
    25	end
    26	
    27	tuples(): () = do
    28	  t1: (ZZ32, ZZ32) = (1, 2)
    29	  t2: (ZZ32, ZZ32) = (1, 2)
    30	  a: Any = t1
    31	  b: Any = t2
    32	  assert(sEq(a, b), "two (1,2)")
    33	end
    34	
    35	strings(): () = do
    36	  s1: String = "ab" || "cd"
    37	  s2: String = "abc" || "d"
    38	  assert(NOT sEq(s1, s2), "two strings built apart")
    39	  assert(sEq(s1, s1), "a string with itself")
    40	end
    41	
    42	objects(): () = do
    43	  p = Pt(1, 2)
    44	  q = Pt(1, 2)
    45	  assert(NOT sEq(p, q), "two Pt(1,2)")
    46	  assert(sEq(p, p), "a Pt with itself")

(* Under walk two string literals of one text are one object, also one literal evaluated twice, a concatenation of string and character literals by || is one literal, and a string built at run time is not SEQV an equal literal. *)
component StringLiteralIdentityWalk
export Executable

ab(): String = "ab"

same(a: Any, b: Any): Boolean = a SEQV b

run(): () = do
    assert("ab" SEQV "ab", "two literals of one text are one object")
    assert(same("ab", "ab"), "two literals of one text are one object at Any")
    assert(ab() SEQV ab(), "one literal evaluated twice is one object")
    x: String = ab()
    y: String = ab()
    assert(same(x, y), "one literal evaluated twice, bound to two variables, is one object")
    assert(("foo" || "bar") SEQV "foobar", "two string literals joined by || are one literal")
    assert(("a" || 'b') SEQV "ab", "a string and a character literal joined by || are one literal")
    assert(("a" || "b" || "c") SEQV "abc", "three string literals joined by || are one literal")
    b: String = "b"
    built: String = "a" || b
    assert(built = "ab", "a string built at run time equals the literal of its text")
    assert(NOT same(built, "ab"), "a string built at run time is not SEQV an equal literal")
    println("PASS")
end

end
EOF

== explorations/coordinator/map/modules-and-phases.md:335-349

## B.5 Desugaring

There are three desugaring phases and they are split by what has to be known, not by which path is running.

PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR must precede name binding because it introduces calls to names (`PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java:39-52`).

PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR produces code that must itself be type-checked: comprehensions and big operators become `__generate`/`__bigOperator`/`__bigOperator2` calls against the library's reduction objects, generator lists become `exp.loop(fn x => body, gs)` chains, and generalized `if`/`while` become `__cond`/`__whileCond` (`PreTypeCheckDesugaringVisitor.java:142-165,245,301,333-335`).

DESUGAR runs after type checking because getter/setter and coercion rewriting need types (`compiler/Desugarer.java:36-45`).

Which visitors run is controlled by `Shell` flags, and this is where the two paths quietly differ: `useInterpreterLibraries` sets `compiled_expr_desugaring` false (`Shell.java:379-386`), so on `walk` the case-expression desugarer (`Desugarer.java:124-127`), the type-ascription desugarer (`:140-144`), the typecase desugarer and the abstract-marking pass (`PreTypeCheckDesugarer.java:117-126`) are all skipped, while coercion and getter/setter desugaring run on both (defaults at `Shell.java:1277,1283`).

`Desugarer.desugarApi` is a no-op — it returns the api unchanged (`compiler/Desugarer.java:82-85`).

After the phase chain, the interpreter runs one more rewrite of its own that the compiler has no counterpart for: `RewriteInPresenceOfTypeInfoVisitor` then `DesugarerVisitor`, which annotate every variable, function and operator reference with its lexical nesting depth (`interpreter/env/ComponentWrapper.java:109-111`, `interpreter/rewrite/DesugarerVisitor.java:30,61-85`). The result is cached in `interpreter_cache` (`ComponentWrapper.java:96,112-114`).

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's distance stage: the compiled checker over the whole interpreter library, the
# fourteen components, the prelude's twelve and the two that List imports, and their apis,
# every stage of every unit run whatever the earlier stages reported, so that nothing hides
# behind an early return; one table.
#
# Why it exists: Pavol's answer 11 (POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-26): the full measurement of the
# distance to the switch-over "becomes a report-only stage of phase 3's gates, whose job is
# driving it down". The checker-count stage beside it (../checker-count/run.sh) sees only
# the errors before each api's early return, 62 of about 1,740 on 2026-09-27.
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir] [setting]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched: the
# shadow sources and classes, the driver, the checker's caches (-Dfortress.caches) and the
# JVM's temporary directory (so Rats! leaves nothing in /tmp) go to the scratch directory
# (default: $TMPDIR or /tmp), and the caches are deleted at the end. It never removes
# /tmp/fortress*rats, which other runs on the machine use. Exit 0 if the table was
# produced, 1 if it could not be. One JVM, -Xmx4g, one busy core: 789 s on the idle 4-CPU
# container on 2026-09-27, 14 to 24 minutes under load 7 to 18 (switch-over-distance-flat.md
# section 5); the table's #seconds and #machine rows say what each run took and where.
#
# The setting: "compile" by default, the compile command's own: DistanceMulti's -setting
# compile takes the extends-Object pre-desugaring from the line that opens
# Shell.useCompilerLibraries() in the tracked ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java,
# read at each run (the run stops, with no total, if that line is not there; its "### order="
# line prints the switch it read, extendsObject=...), and turns the compiled-expression
# desugaring on, as the compile path does. Answer 11 names the compile path's setting. That
# line sets the switch off, the implicit bound Any of P-42 (row 412), so the default runs as
# "any", which fixes the switch off whatever Shell.java says; with the switch on, the compile
# setting gave 685 errors on climb batch 22's code, 580 on the bound Object (F-289). "any"
# differs from walk's setting by the compiled-expression desugaring: on the tree of 2026-09-27
# 1,746 to 1,747 errors against 1,737 to 1,738 (FACTS.md, "The true distance to the
# switch-over"). The third argument, any or walk, runs another setting, for a comparison
# with the measurements on file; the gate never passes it.
#
# The overloading checker's memo is off (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false), as in
# every run of the measurement: keyed on declaration pairs, it hides 27 to 35 errors
# depending on the build order (FACTS.md, "The overloading checker's memo hides errors
# by build order, so every count runs with it off ...").
#
# The sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-27, so that the gate does not
# depend on a probe directory, as the checker-count stage's were: DistanceMulti.java from
# perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance-flat/ (35ef70584); shadow-patch.py from
# perf-probes/prelude/desugar-codegen/ (e5d8cdbd2); add-patch.py and errors.py from
# perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance/ (a7e3df9ad, 14d2f9839); classify.py from
# perf-probes/prelude/distance-triage/ (e17a9badc); all unchanged but classify.py, which since
# row 577 finds the library places that name three of its classes by their declarations in
# the tree's sources ($FH, passed to table.py), not by line ranges. table.py is new: it
# counts as those scripts count and prints the rows below. The shadow classes are not
# copies: they are made from the tracked sources at every run by text edits that must each
# match exactly once (shadow-patch.py, add-patch.py), so there is no copied checker to go
# stale silently; an edit that no longer matches stops the run before the checker starts,
# and the table then says so in its #shadow row, with no counts.
#
# The table, tab-separated, every row tagged:
#   #distance   the setting, the switches and the fourteen targets
#   #total      distinct errors; or "none:" and why, when no total was measured, as when a

StrictEquivalenceRuleWalk and StrictEquivalenceRuleCompiled build their
strings apart with a variable operand, which the fold leaves, so they keep

1	(* Under walk, a program's own builtinPrimitive binding of a glue class over String receives a non-flat string's type name in place of its characters. *)
     2	component NativeGlueNonFlatStringWalk
     3	export Executable
     4	
     5	env(name:String, defaultValue:String):String = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.StringPrim$GetEnvironment")
     6	
     7	run():() = do
     8	  s: String = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz" || "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"
     9	  unset: String = "FORTRESS_NO_SUCH_VARIABLE_OR_PROPERTY"
    10	  assert(|s|, 52, "|s|")
    11	  assert(s.depth, 1, "the concatenation is a rope")
    12	  assert(env(unset, s.asFlatString), s.asFlatString, "the glue at the flat string answers its characters")
    13	  assert(env(unset, s), "CatString", "the glue at the non-flat string answers its type name CatString")
    14	end
    15	
    16	end
(* Under walk, getEnvironment, getProperty and the three thread prints read the characters of a rope made by ||, a SubString and EmptyString, and match those of flat strings. *)
component NativeHelperStringRopeWalk
import String.{CatString, SubString, EmptyString}
import System.{getEnvironment, getProperty}
export Executable

isSubString(s: String): Boolean = typecase s of
    SubString => true
    else => false
  end

run():() = do
  long: String = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz" || "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"
  assert(|long|, 52, "|long|")
  assert(long.depth, 1, "the concatenation is a rope")
  unset: String = "FORTRESS_NO_SUCH_VARIABLE_OR_PROPERTY"

  pathFlat = getEnvironment("PATH", "?")
  assert(pathFlat =/= "?", true, "PATH is set")
  pathRope: String = CatString("PA", "TH")
  pathWide: String = CatString("xPA", "THx")
  pathSub: String = pathWide[1#4]
  assert(isSubString(pathSub), true, "pathSub is a SubString")
  assert(getEnvironment(pathRope, "?"), pathFlat, "getEnvironment at a rope name")
  assert(getEnvironment(pathSub, "?"), pathFlat, "getEnvironment at a SubString name")
  assert(getEnvironment(unset, long), long.asFlatString, "getEnvironment at a rope default")
  assert(getEnvironment(unset, pathSub), "PATH", "getEnvironment at a SubString default")
  assert(getEnvironment(unset, EmptyString), "", "getEnvironment at an EmptyString default")
  assert(getEnvironment(EmptyString, "?"), "?", "getEnvironment at an EmptyString name")

  versionFlat = getProperty("java.version", "?")
  assert(versionFlat =/= "?", true, "java.version is set")
  versionRope: String = CatString("java.", "version")
  versionWide: String = CatString("xjava.", "versionx")
  versionSub: String = versionWide[1#12]
  assert(isSubString(versionSub), true, "versionSub is a SubString")
  assert(getProperty(versionRope, "?"), versionFlat, "getProperty at a rope name")
  assert(getProperty(versionSub, "?"), versionFlat, "getProperty at a SubString name")
  assert(getProperty(unset, long), long.asFlatString, "getProperty at a rope default")
  assert(getProperty(unset, versionSub), "java.version", "getProperty at a SubString default")

    10	charactersOf(name: String): ZZ32 = SUM[\ZZ32\][c <- FileReadStream(name).characters()] 1
    11	
    12	consumedRead(r: ReadStream): String =

    15	    "read " || s

    19
